slides.title: Do QR codes **expire?**
slides.sub: Short answer: the code doesn't. The service behind it might.

slides.title: A static code never expires
slides.body: It stores your link or text directly in the pattern. It scans for as long as the print survives.

slides.title: So why do codes stop working?
slides.body: Almost always it's the service behind a dynamic code: a free trial runs out, a plan is cancelled or a domain lapses.

items: What happens if I stop paying?

Can I export my codes and scans?

posts.caption:

QR codes themselves don't expire. A static code stores your link right in the pattern, so it works as long as the print does.

When a code "dies", it's usually the service behind a dynamic code: a free trial ended, a plan was cancelled or a domain lapsed.

slides.title: How big should a QR code **be?**
slides.sub: Use the 10:1 rule.

slides.label: Scan distance : code width
slides.body: Scanned from 2 m away? Make the code at least 20 cm wide.

slides.title: Save this for your **next print**

posts.caption:
The 10:1 rule for QR codes 📏

Your code should be at least 1/10 as wide as the distance people scan it from.

📇 Business card → 2 cm
📄 Flyer → 3 cm
🍽️ Table tent → 5 cm
🪧 Poster at 1 m → 10 cm
🎪 Banner at 5 m → 50 cm

Treat these as minimums. Go bigger in bad light or if people scan at an angle.

Static or dynamic QR code? Here's the whole difference in one picture 👆

✅ Static: free, fixed, works forever. Great for WiFi, contact cards and links that won't change.
✅ Dynamic: you can change where it points after printing and see how many people scan it. Great for menus, posters and campaigns.

Which one do you use most? Tell us below 👇

slides.title: QR code not **scanning?**
slides.sub: 5 causes behind most failures, and the fix for each.

slides.title: Low contrast
slides.body: Scanners see brightness, not colour. If the code blends in when you squint, make the modules darker or the background lighter.

slides.title: Inverted colours
slides.body: Light modules on a dark background fail on some phones. Use dark modules on a light background.

slides.title: No quiet zone
slides.body: Keep a plain margin 4 modules wide on every side. Text or borders too close break it.

slides.title: Logo too big
slides.body: Keep a logo to about 20 to 25% of the code's area, away from the 3 corner squares.

slides.title: Too small
slides.body: Use the 10:1 rule: the code should be 1/10 of the scanning distance.

slides.body: Every QR code needs a plain, light margin 4 modules wide on every side. It's how the scanner finds where the code starts.

slides.title: How much damage can a QR code **survive?**
slides.body: Higher levels are tougher but make the code denser. Adding a logo? Use H.

posts.caption:
A QR code can still scan with part of it missing 🤯

That's error correction. There are 4 levels:
L → ~7%
M → ~15%
Q → ~25%
H → ~30%

Higher = tougher, but denser. If you put a logo in the middle, use H (our free generator switches to H automatically when you add a logo).
